voice_over: Antarctica. A seal rests on a slab of floating ice. It is out of the water. It should be safe.
visual: Wide shot of pack ice, a seal on a floe. Wind, distant ice creaking.

voice_over: Then the fins appear. Five, six, seven of them, lined up side by side.
visual: Black dorsal fins breaking the surface in a row. Low drone.

voice_over: They don't attack the ice. They swim at it, together, and dive at the last second. A wave rises behind them and rolls across the floe.
visual: Orcas swimming in formation; water surging over ice. Music hit.

voice_over: The seal slides. Once. Twice. The hunters turn and come again.
visual: Repeated waves washing over ice.

voice_over: This is not instinct. It is a technique. It has to be learned, practised and passed on, from one generation to the next.
visual: Slow motion: orca surfacing, eye visible.

voice_over: And it is only one of many hunting traditions, spread across the oceans of the world, all practised by a single animal.
visual: Montage: orcas in polar, tropical and temperate waters.

voice_over: What if the most dangerous predator in the sea is not just a hunter… but a culture?
visual: [3 s — music swell] Title: ORCAS — THE OCEAN'S WOLF PACKS

voice_over: The orca, or killer whale, is not really a whale in the way we usually picture one. It is the largest member of the oceanic dolphin family.
visual: Orca swimming alongside dolphins (or cut between the two).

voice_over: It can grow to nearly ten metres long and weigh up to ten tonnes. Females can live an estimated eighty to ninety years. Males, fifty to sixty.
visual: Size comparison graphic: orca next to a diver and a bus.

voice_over: Orcas live in every ocean on Earth, from the polar ice to the tropics. And almost nothing in the sea is safe from them: fish, seals, sea lions, sharks, even other whales.
visual: Map graphic, then quick cuts of prey species.

voice_over: But here is the strange part. No single orca eats all of these things.
visual: Close-up of a single orca. [2 s pause]

voice_over: Each population has its own menu, its own hunting methods and its own social life. They share the same body, but they live in completely different worlds.
visual: Split screen: two different orca groups.

voice_over: Scientists call these groups ecotypes. And to understand them, we have to start where orcas have been studied longer than anywhere else: the coast of the North Pacific.
visual: Aerial shot of a rocky coastline with forest.

voice_over: Over the next twenty minutes, we will meet eight of these orca worlds. Some hunt with waves. Some hunt on land. One pair has driven the ocean's most famous shark from its own coastline.
visual: Fast teaser cuts of each chapter.

voice_over: By the end, you may never see the word "killer" in quite the same way again.
visual: Orca blowing at the surface at sunset.

voice_over: Chapter one: the orcas that never mix.
visual: Title card "1 — Two worlds, one sea".

voice_over: In the 1970s, a Canadian scientist named Michael Bigg began studying the orcas off British Columbia, learning to recognise each whale by the shape of its dorsal fin.
visual: Dorsal fin ID graphic.

voice_over: He noticed something odd. In the very same waters, there were two kinds of orcas. And they did not mix.
visual: Two groups of orcas passing at a distance.

voice_over: The first kind lived in large, tight family groups and ate fish, almost always salmon. Today they are known as residents.
visual: Orcas surfacing in a family group; salmon underwater.

voice_over: The second kind roamed in smaller groups and ignored the salmon entirely. They hunted seals, sea lions and other whales. Today they carry his name: Bigg's killer whales.
visual: Small group of orcas near a seal haul-out.

voice_over: Side by side, they look almost identical. But genetic studies suggest the two lines split more than three hundred thousand years ago.
visual: Graphic: family tree with two branches far apart.

voice_over: In 2024, a team of researchers proposed that they are not one species at all, but two, with two separate scientific names: Orcinus ater for the residents, and Orcinus rectipinnus for Bigg's.
visual: Text on screen: Orcinus ater / Orcinus rectipinnus.

voice_over: The scientific community has not fully agreed. That same year, the Society for Marine Mammalogy recognised them as two subspecies, but stopped short of calling them separate species.
visual: Neutral ocean shot.

voice_over: Either way, the lesson is clear. To an orca, what you eat, how you hunt and who you travel with is not a detail. It defines who you are.
visual: Close-up of an orca eye.

voice_over: And nowhere is that more obvious than at the bottom of the world.
visual: Transition to icy water.

voice_over: Chapter two: the wave makers.
visual: Title card "2 — The wave makers".

voice_over: In the waters around the Antarctic Peninsula, scientists from the United States' National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration followed a group they called pack ice killer whales.
visual: Antarctic coastline, research vessel (generic).

voice_over: These orcas specialise in seals resting on floating ice. And they have solved a problem that should be impossible for an animal that cannot leave the water.
visual: Seal on ice floe, orca fin circling.

voice_over: First, they find a seal. Several orcas rise and look at it, heads above the surface. Researchers call this spy-hopping.
visual: Orca head rising vertically out of the water.

voice_over: Then they back off, line up, and charge the floe together, beating their tails. Just before impact, they dive. The water they push forward keeps going, as a wave.
visual: Formation swimming; surge of water over ice.

voice_over: If the seal holds on, they do it again. And again. The researchers saw groups repeat the attack for half an hour or more. Every wave costs energy. Every wave has to be timed together. This is coordination, not chance.
visual: Repeated wave sequence, sped up.

voice_over: And here is the detail that surprised everyone. Among the seals resting on the ice, Weddell seals made up only around fifteen percent. Yet in the kills the team recorded, fourteen out of fifteen were Weddell seals.
visual: Graphic: 15% of seals on ice → 14 of 15 kills.

voice_over: The orcas were not taking whatever they found. They were choosing. Why they prefer Weddell seals is still unknown.
visual: Weddell seal on ice, close-up.

voice_over: A wave as a weapon. Teamwork as a tool. But some orcas take an even bigger risk. They leave the ocean altogether.
visual: Waves crashing on a beach.

voice_over: Chapter three: the beach raiders.
visual: Title card "3 — The beach raiders".

voice_over: Punta Norte, in Argentine Patagonia. Every year, sea lion colonies on these pebble beaches fill with pups.
visual: Sea lion colony on a beach, pups at the water's edge.

voice_over: In March and April, the youngest pups start to play in the shallows. They are clumsy, slow, and very close to the waves.
visual: Pups splashing in shallow surf.

voice_over: Out at sea, a tall black fin is waiting.
visual: Single dorsal fin in the surf line. Tension music.

voice_over: Then the orca does something no ocean predator should do. It rides a wave straight onto the beach, grabs a pup, and twists its body to slide back into the sea.
visual: Orca surging onto sand (stock if available; otherwise wave + fin + reaction shots).

voice_over: It is extremely dangerous. An orca that misjudges the wave can end up stuck on the sand, where its own weight could kill it.
visual: Heavy surf, slow motion.

voice_over: This is why the technique has to be taught. A local ranger reported that only seven orcas here were known to hunt this way, and only five of them taught it to younger whales.
visual: Adult orca and young orca swimming together.

voice_over: Young orcas have been seen following an experienced hunter, staying close to the beach, sharing the catch, practising without fully committing.
visual: Young orca in shallow water near an adult.

voice_over: That same ranger called it a culture at risk. If the few teachers disappear, the knowledge disappears with them.
visual: Wide shot of empty beach at dusk.

voice_over: Small prey, big risk. But some orcas have gone in the opposite direction. They hunt the biggest animal that has ever lived.
visual: Deep blue water, huge shadow passing below.

voice_over: Chapter four: hunting a giant.
visual: Title card "4 — Hunting a giant".

voice_over: The blue whale. Around twenty metres long or more. The largest animal ever known to have existed. For a long time, scientists doubted that anything could kill a healthy adult.
visual: Blue whale swimming (NOAA / stock).

voice_over: In March 2019, off the south coast of Western Australia, researchers on a boat near a deep-sea canyon watched it happen.
visual: Open ocean off a rugged coast.

voice_over: A dozen or so orcas had found a blue whale. They had been chasing it for a long time.
visual: Orca fins surrounding a large back. Dramatic music.

voice_over: The orcas bit into its body and flanks. Two of them pushed onto the whale, forcing it under, until it could no longer breathe.
visual: Graphic recreation or fast cuts, no gore.

voice_over: Then, more orcas arrived. Around fifty gathered to share the carcass.
visual: Many fins at the surface.

voice_over: Strangely, the first thing they ate was the tongue, probably while the whale was still alive. Nobody knows why it is their preferred cut.
visual: Slow push over dark water, no gore.

voice_over: It was not a one-off. By 2021, the same research team had documented three separate blue whale kills in the area, published in the journal Marine Mammal Science.
visual: Text on screen: 3 kills, 2019–2021.

voice_over: One of the researchers said it raised the bar higher than he had ever imagined. And as blue whale numbers slowly recover from whaling, these hunts may become more common.
visual: Blue whale diving, tail up.

voice_over: But the most dramatic orca story of the last decade is not about size. It is about two individuals. And a fish that every swimmer fears.
visual: Shark silhouette in murky water.

voice_over: Chapter five: the shark hunters.
visual: Title card "5 — Port and Starboard".

voice_over: For decades, the coast of South Africa was famous for one thing: great white sharks. Tourists came from around the world to see them from cages.
visual: Great white shark swimming (stock).

voice_over: Then, starting around 2015, dead great whites began washing up on the beaches. Each one had the same wound. And each one was missing the same organ: its liver.
visual: Empty beach; graphic of a shark with liver highlighted.

voice_over: The shark's liver is huge and rich in oil. For a predator, it is pure energy.
visual: Graphic: liver as a large share of body.

voice_over: The prime suspects were two male orcas, easy to recognise because their tall dorsal fins had collapsed. One bends to the left, one to the right.
visual: Two orca fins, one bent left, one bent right (graphic).

voice_over: Like the sides of a ship, they were named Port and Starboard. They had first been reported in 2009, off the coast of Namibia, long before anyone connected them to the dead sharks.
visual: Text on screen: PORT · STARBOARD.

voice_over: At least seven dead great whites were found in 2017 alone. Within a few years, great white sightings in some of their favourite bays dropped to almost nothing.
visual: Graph line falling to zero (simple graphic).

voice_over: The ocean's most famous predator had been pushed off its own coastline. In some places, shark cage diving, a whole local industry built around great whites, came to a stop.
visual: Empty shark-diving cage at the surface.

voice_over: Then, in June 2023, researchers saw something new. Starboard, alone, caught a young great white and killed it in less than two minutes. Then he swam past their boat carrying a piece of its liver. The next day, a second, larger great white washed up nearby, also without its liver, probably from an earlier attack nobody saw.
visual: Single fin, fast movement, splash.

voice_over: The pair have also killed other shark species. On a single day in February 2023, at least seventeen sevengill sharks were found dead off the same coast, livers removed.
visual: Sevengill shark (stock).

voice_over: Scientists still don't know why these two started hunting sharks, or whether others will learn from them. But in the world of orcas, a new habit can spread.
visual: Two fins side by side, sunset.

voice_over: And the ones who guide what the group knows, it turns out, are not the biggest males.
visual: Older female orca surfacing.

voice_over: Chapter six: the grandmothers.
visual: Title card "6 — The grandmothers". Warm music.

voice_over: Very few animals go through menopause. Humans do. And, as far as we know, only five other species do: all of them toothed whales. Orcas are one of them.
visual: Text: Humans + 5 toothed whales (orca, false killer whale, short-finned pilot whale, beluga, narwhal).

voice_over: A female orca stops having calves partway through her life. But she can live for decades afterwards.
visual: Older female with younger orcas.

voice_over: For a long time, that made no evolutionary sense. Why live so long if you can no longer reproduce?
visual: Slow drift underwater.

voice_over: Researchers from the University of Exeter found part of the answer by studying the resident orcas of the North Pacific over decades.
visual: Family group swimming together.

voice_over: When salmon are scarce, older post-menopausal females are more likely to lead the group as it travels and searches for food. They seem to carry the knowledge of where the fish can be found, built up over a lifetime of good years and bad ones.
visual: Matriarch at the front of a group; salmon run footage.

voice_over: In a 2019 study of almost four hundred young orcas, calves whose grandmother had died in the previous two years had a mortality rate four and a half times higher than calves with a living grandmother.
visual: Graphic: 4.5× higher mortality.

voice_over: And in 2024, a comparison of toothed whale species found that females in species with menopause live around forty years longer than females of similar species without it.
visual: Graphic: lifespan bars.

voice_over: The extra years are not wasted. They are spent leading, protecting and teaching.
visual: Grandmother orca beside a calf. [3 s — music]

voice_over: In a society built on knowledge, the elders are the library. And when a member of the family dies, these whales seem to feel it.
visual: Calm water, family group surfacing slowly.

voice_over: Chapter seven: a mother's grief.
visual: Title card "7 — Seventeen days". Slow strings.

voice_over: On July twenty-fourth, 2018, off the coast of British Columbia, a female resident orca known as Tahlequah, or J35, gave birth to a calf.
visual: Calm sea, misty coastline.

voice_over: The calf died within about half an hour.
visual: [2 s — silence]

voice_over: But Tahlequah did not let go. She pushed the body ahead of her, balancing it on her head, and carried it as the family travelled.
visual: Orca surfacing slowly, pushing something ahead (generic, respectful).

voice_over: Day after day. A week. Two weeks. Other members of her pod were seen taking turns carrying the calf.
visual: Day counter on screen: Day 1… Day 10…

voice_over: She carried it for about seventeen days, over roughly one thousand six hundred kilometres. Then she let it go, and rejoined her family.
visual: Wide aerial of open water. Day 17.

voice_over: The world watched. And many people asked a question science is still careful with: was this grief?
visual: Orca eye, close-up.

voice_over: We cannot know what an orca feels. But we can see what she does. And at the very end of 2024, she did it again. A new calf, a female, died within days, and Tahlequah was seen carrying her body into the new year.
visual: Grey winter sea.

voice_over: Her story is also the story of her population. And that population is in trouble.
visual: Coastal city skyline across the water.

voice_over: Tahlequah belongs to the Southern Residents, a community of orcas that lives around the waters between Washington State and British Columbia.
visual: Map graphic: Salish Sea.

voice_over: They depend on one kind of fish above all: Chinook salmon. And Chinook salmon have declined.
visual: Salmon swimming upstream; dam in the background.

voice_over: In 1995, there were ninety-eight Southern Residents. By the end of 2021, there were seventy-three. They are listed as endangered in both the United States and Canada.
visual: Graphic: 98 → 73.

voice_over: Their waters are also contaminated by pollutants that build up in the bodies of top predators.
visual: Industrial shoreline, murky water.

voice_over: There is some good news. The 2026 census counted seventy-six Southern Residents, the second year in a row with a small increase. And in October 2026, a new calf was spotted, bringing the count to seventy-seven. Researchers and governments have argued for years over how to help them, from removing dams to restoring salmon runs.
visual: Graphic: 76 in 2026, up arrow.

voice_over: Seventy-seven whales. Small enough that every birth and every death changes the future of the whole community.
visual: Family group surfacing together.

voice_over: Meanwhile, on the other side of the Atlantic, another tiny orca population has made headlines for a very different reason.
visual: Sailboat on blue water, Strait of Gibraltar.

voice_over: Chapter eight: the rudder raiders.
visual: Title card "8 — The rudder raiders". Playful but tense music.

voice_over: Since 2020, sailors off the coasts of Spain and Portugal have reported a strange encounter. A group of orcas approaches a sailboat, goes straight for the rudder, and pushes, bites and spins it.
visual: Sailboat from above, fins approaching the stern.

voice_over: More than seven hundred interactions have been logged. At least eight boats have sunk.
visual: Text on screen: 700+ interactions · 8+ boats sunk.

voice_over: Online, the story became a revenge tale: orcas fighting back against humans. Most scientists studying them do not support that idea.
visual: Generic, invented social-media headlines, blurred.

voice_over: The Iberian orca population is tiny, fewer than fifty animals, and considered critically endangered. Only around fifteen of them have been involved in the incidents.
visual: Small group of orcas.

voice_over: The leading explanation is social learning. Young orcas seem to copy the rudder behaviour from older ones, and the habit has spread through the group, the way a game spreads through a playground.
visual: Young orca following an adult.

voice_over: It may have started with one bad encounter with a boat. It may have no deeper meaning at all. But it shows, once again, how fast an idea can travel through an orca society.
visual: Rudder close-up, water rushing.

voice_over: And that brings us back to the question at the start of this film.
visual: Orca surfacing, slow motion.

voice_over: Wave makers in Antarctica. Beach hunters in Patagonia. Blue whale hunters in Australia. Shark hunters in South Africa. Salmon specialists in the North Pacific. Rudder spinners in Spain.
visual: Rapid montage of each chapter's best shot.

voice_over: Physically, they are almost the same animal. What separates them is what they have learned.
visual: Close-up of an orca eye.

voice_over: Their hunting methods are passed from one generation to the next. Their food preferences are traditions. Their knowledge is carried by the oldest females.
visual: Grandmother orca with family.

voice_over: That is what many scientists mean when they say orcas have culture. Not art, not language as we know it, but behaviour that is learned socially and shared within a group.
visual: Group of orcas breathing together at the surface.

voice_over: And culture can be fragile. When a population shrinks, it can lose more than individuals. It can lose a way of life, a technique, a map of where food can be found.
visual: Empty sea at dusk.

voice_over: The Patagonian beach hunters depend on a handful of teachers. The Southern Residents depend on salmon, and on the rivers where salmon are born. The Iberian orcas number fewer than fifty. Each of these cultures hangs by a thread, and each thread is different.
visual: Three-part split screen.

voice_over: Protecting orcas is not just about saving a species. It is about saving many different ways of being an orca.
visual: Wide shot of a pod travelling.

voice_over: We gave them a frightening name: killer whale.
visual: Orca breaching, slow motion.

voice_over: But watch them long enough and a different picture appears. Families that travel together. Grandmothers who lead. Mothers who will not let go.
visual: Family group, grandmother, Tahlequah callback shot.

voice_over: Hunters, yes. Perhaps the most skilled hunters in the ocean. But also teachers, students and keepers of traditions passed down for generations.
visual: Orca spy-hopping, looking at the camera.

voice_over: Out there, right now, a young orca is watching its elders, learning how its family has always survived.
visual: Young orca beside an adult in clear water.

voice_over: The question is whether we will leave enough ocean for those lessons to be passed on.
visual: Pod disappearing into the distance. [4 s — music resolves]

voice_over: If you enjoyed this film, subscribe to Naturexplore: a new documentary every Wednesday. And tell us in the comments: which orca tradition surprised you most?
visual: End card with two suggested videos, including The Octopus: An Alien Mind.
